questions.knowledge_point: Finding the First Few Terms for the Derivative of a Taylor Series
questions.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=1$ is given by

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{5n-1}(x-1)^{n}.
$$

Calculate the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor series expansion about $x=1$ of ${f}^{′}(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Writing the first few terms of the series explicitly, we have

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{4}{5n-1}(x-1)^{n}=(x-1)+\frac{4}{9}(x-1)^{2}+\frac{2}{7}(x-1)^{3}+⋯.
$$

To find ${f}^{′}(x),$ we differentiate term-by-term. This gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=1+\frac{8}{9}(x-1)+\frac{6}{7}(x-1)^{2}+⋯.
$$

questions.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-1)^{n-1}\frac{{x}^{n+1}}{{2}^{n}}.
$$

Calculate the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor series expansion about $x=0$ of ${f}^{′}(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Writing the first few terms of the series explicitly, we have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-1)^{n-1}\frac{{x}^{n+1}}{{2}^{n}}=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{4}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{8}-⋯.
$$

To find ${f}^{′}(x),$ we differentiate term-by-term. This gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=x-\frac{3{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}-⋯.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the a General Term for the Derivative of a Taylor Series
questions.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=3$ is given by

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-1)^{n+1}\frac{n(x-3)^{n}}{n+3}.
$$

Find ${a}_{n},$ given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-1)^{n+1}{a}_{n}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Writing the terms of the series explicitly, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{4}(x-3)-\frac{2}{5}(x-3)^{2}+⋯+{{(-1)^{n+1}\frac{n(x-3)^{n}}{n+3}}_{⏟}}_{\text{the }n\text{th term}}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above series term-by-term gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{4}{5}(x-3)+⋯+{{(-1)^{n+1}\frac{{n}^{2}(x-3)^{n-1}}{n+3}}_{⏟}}_{\text{the }n\text{th term}}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the Taylor series for ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the sigma notation as follows:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-1)^{n+1}\frac{{n}^{2}(x-3)^{n-1}}{n+3}
$$

Comparing the series above with the given series, we can deduce that

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{2}(x-3)^{n-1}}{n+3}.
$$

$$

Differentiating the above series term-by-term gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{6}-\frac{2x}{120}+⋯+{{\frac{(-1)^{n+1}n{x}^{n-1}}{(2n+1)!}}_{⏟}}_{\text{the }n\text{th term}}+⋯.

questions.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=-2$ is given by

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-1)^{n}\frac{(x+2)^{n+1}}{n!}.
$$

Find ${a}_{n},$ given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-1)^{n}{a}_{n}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Writing the terms of the series explicitly, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-(x+2)^{2}+\frac{1}{2!}(x+2)^{3}-⋯+{{(-1)^{n}\frac{(x+2)^{n+1}}{n!}}_{⏟}}_{\text{the }n\text{th term}}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above series term-by-term gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =-2(x+2)+\frac{3}{2!}(x+2)^{2}-⋯+{{(-1)^{n}\frac{(n+1)(x+2)^{n}}{n!}}_{⏟}}_{\text{the }n\text{th term}}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the Taylor series for ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the sigma notation as follows:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-1)^{n}\frac{(n+1)(x+2)^{n}}{n!}
$$

Comparing the series above with the given series, we can deduce that

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{(n+1)(x+2)^{n}}{n!}.
$$

questions.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=1$ is given by 

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }(-2)^{k}(x-1)^{k+1}.
$$

Find ${a}_{k},$ given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }{a}_{k}(-2)^{k}(x-1)^{k}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Writing the terms of the series explicitly, we have

$$
f(x)=-2(x-1)^{2}+4(x-1)^{3}-⋯+{{(-2)^{k}(x-1)^{k+1}}_{⏟}}_{\text{the }k\text{th term}}+⋯.
$$

Differentiating the above series term-by-term gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=-4(x-1)+12(x-1)^{2}-⋯+{{(k+1)(-2)^{k}(x-1)^{k}}_{⏟}}_{\text{the }k\text{th term}}+⋯.
$$

We can now write the Taylor series for ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the sigma notation as follows:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)={\sum }_{k=1}^{\infty }(k+1)(-2)^{k}(x-1)^{k}
$$

Comparing the series above with the given series, we can deduce that

$$
{a}_{k}=k+1.
$$

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\,{x}^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}.

${f}^{′}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }$

$$
f(x)={x}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+⋯+{{\frac{2\,{x}^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}}_{⏟}}_{\text{the }n\text{th term}}+⋯.
$$

Differentiating the above series term-by-term gives

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Radius of Convergence for the Derivative of a Taylor Series
questions.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{2}^{n}{x}^{n}.
$$

The series converges to $f(x)$ for $|x|<R,$ where $R$ is the radius of convergence of the Taylor series. Calculate the radius of convergence of the series expansion of ${f}^{′}(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ about $x=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
The radius of convergence for the Taylor series of ${f}^{′}(x)$ is the same as the Taylor series of $f(x).$ So, to find the radius of convergence of ${f}^{′}(x),$ we need to compute $R.$

To calculate $R,$ we can use the ratio test. Computing the limit of the absolute value of the ratio of two consecutive terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{2}^{n+1}{x}^{n+1}}{{2}^{n}{x}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|2x| \\  & =2|x|.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The series converges when $L<1.$ So, it converges when

$$
\begin{aligned}2|x| & <1 \\ |x| & <\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of convergence is $R=\frac{1}{2}.$

questions.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{2n}}{{2}^{2n}(n!)^{2}}.
$$

The series converges to $f(x)$ for $|x|<R,$ where $R$ is the radius of convergence of the Taylor series. Calculate the radius of convergence of the series expansion of ${f}^{′}(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ about $x=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
The radius of convergence for the Taylor series of ${f}^{′}(x)$ is the same as the Taylor series of $f(x).$ So, to find the radius of convergence of ${f}^{′}(x),$ we need to compute $R.$

To calculate $R,$ we can use the ratio test. Computing the limit of the absolute value of the ratio of two consecutive terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{x}^{2n+2}}{{2}^{2n+2}((n+1)!)^{2}}\cdot \frac{{2}^{2n}(n!)^{2}}{{x}^{2n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}(n+1)^{2}}| \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\cdot {lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{1}{(n+1)^{2}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The series converges when $L<1.$ Since $0<1$ for all $x,$ we conclude that $R=\infty .$

questions.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{{2}^{n}n}.
$$

The series converges to $f(x)$ for $|x|<R,$ where $R$ is the radius of convergence of the Taylor series. Calculate the radius of convergence of the series expansion of ${f}^{′}(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ about $x=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
The radius of convergence for the Taylor series of ${f}^{′}(x)$ is the same as the Taylor series of $f(x).$ So, to find the radius of convergence of ${f}^{′}(x),$ we need to compute $R.$

To calculate $R,$ we can use the ratio test. Computing the limit of the absolute value of the ratio of two consecutive terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{x}^{n+1}}{{2}^{n+1}(n+1)}\cdot \frac{{2}^{n}n}{{x}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{xn}{2(n+1)}| \\  & =\frac{|x|}{2}\cdot {lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{1}{(1+\frac{1}{n})} \\  & =\frac{|x|}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The series converges when $L<1.$ So, it converges when

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{|x|}{2} & <1 \\ |x| & <2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of convergence is $R=2.$

questions.problem:
The Taylor series for the function $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by

$$
f(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\sqrt{n}\,{x}^{n}.
$$

The series converges to $f(x)$ for $|x|<R,$ where $R$ is the radius of convergence of the Taylor series. Calculate the radius of convergence of the series expansion of ${f}^{′}(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ about $x=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
The radius of convergence for the Taylor series of ${f}^{′}(x)$ is the same as the Taylor series of $f(x).$ So, to find the radius of convergence of ${f}^{′}(x),$ we need to compute $R.$

To calculate $R,$ we can use the ratio test. Computing the limit of the absolute value of the ratio of two consecutive terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{\sqrt{n+1}\,{x}^{n+1}}{\sqrt{n}\,{x}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|x\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{n}}| \\  & =|x|.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The series converges when $L<1.$ So, it converges when

$$
\begin{aligned}|x| & <1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of convergence is $R=1.$
